newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Mobutu says he seeks only national unity.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu says he seeks only national unity.

text.p: Ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, his hold over Zaire crumbling as rebel foes advance, has stepped back into the spotlight saying his wants to preserve the sprawling nation's unity and territorial integrity.

Mobutu, who left hospital in Europe last week after fresh cancer treatment, told journalists on Sunday he expected to make clear his plans within 48 hours. It was his first public outing since his return on Friday.

The United States and Belgium, the former colonial power, meanwhile, sent troops to the region, ready to rescue their citizens should that prove necessary. France has already sent troops to neighbouring Congo and Gabon for the same reason.

In the southern mining capital of Lubumbashi, residents reported that members of Mobutu's presidential guard had flown in to defend the city and had increased their patrols. The rebels say Lubumbashi -- Elisabethville in Belgian colonial days -- is one of their next major targets.

Wearing his trade-mark leopard skin hat and carrying his habitual cane, Mobutu looked tired and drawn but walked unaided as he met the world's press before taking delivery of a letter from South Africa's Nelson Mandela.

"I have returned not to devote myself to Mobutu's interests or Mobutu's fortune as you write from time to time but to the higher interests of Zaire," he said with characteristic irony. "That is to say our unity, our territorial integrity."
Asked about his plans, he replied: "In the next 48 hours you will know."
Mandela's deputy Thabo Mbeki, who delivered the letter, said afterwards that a U.N. peace plan for a truce and talks was at the heart of efforts to end Zaire's five-month-old civil war.
"We are convinced that in the immediate future steps will be taken practically to move the peace process forward towards a resolution," Mbeki told reporters.
Mbeki managed a bid by Mandela to broker peace between Mobutu and the rebels in South Africa last month.

Mobutu, 66, has ruled Zaire since an army coup in 1965. Many Zaireans, ground down by three decades of poverty and hardship, are eager for a change and are openly rallying to rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
Mobutu has spent most of his time in Europe since prostate cancer surgery in August.
Kabila, his popularity rising with each rebel victory, called on Saturday for a transitional government but said he would not work with anyone who had shared power with Mobutu.
Before leaving France for home, Mobutu called for a truce and talks and the creation of a national council to find ways out of the crisis "with all our brothers, without exclusion".

Kabila says talks must come first. His forces, who took up arms in October and control a fifth of Zaire, say they have pushed south to within 200 km (125 miles) of Lubumbashi, capital of autonomy-hungry Shaba.
Lubumbashi residents say many of the several hundred soldiers guarding the city are locals who have told friends they will not put up a fight.
The rebels say they are 100 km (60 miles) from the diamond city of Mbuji-Mayi -- their second immediate target to the north east.
